title: Block close: letters to you
hookLine: the letters were written to real churches, and churches still read them as addressed to them
tomorrow: a short old book opens at a fork in the road. which way?

lines: A LETTER TO YOUR FUTURE SELF.
TO ALL THAT BE IN ROME.
cards: Some people write a letter to their future self and seal it, or schedule an email to land years from now. The person who opens it won't quite be the person who wrote it.

Romans has an address on it: "To all that be in Rome, beloved of God, called to be saints." Real people, in a real city, waiting for news. Nobody in that room was writing to a stranger far down the road.
So who is that letter addressed to now?

teach.h: EVERY LETTER HAD A FIRST READER.
teach.b: Look back over this stretch: a scribe named Tertius, hymns caught on the page, household codes read in context, a page of hellos full of co-workers. Every letter went to someone else first. Romans to Rome.
Philemon to one man, about one brother. So how do churches read other people's mail? The letters open that door themselves.

teach.h: IN EVERY PLACE, THEIRS AND OURS.
teach.b: First Corinthians is written "Unto the church of God which is at Corinth," and then the address widens: "with all that in every place call upon the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, both theirs and ours." Every place.

Colossians asks to be passed along: "when this epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans." A letter for one town, read aloud in the next. Churches have kept doing that.
Read in worship, the letters are heard as addressed to whoever is sitting there. That doesn't erase Corinth. Reading in context means remembering who opened the letter first.
Reading as if to you means letting it open you too.

teach.h: CONTEXT AND YOU, BOTH AT ONCE.

teach.b: And tomorrow a new block begins: the saints and teachers who came after, in their own words.

how: Churches read a passage from the letters in many Sunday services, introduced by the name of the church it was first sent to, and preach on it as words for the people in the room.

games.q: letters with addresses — tap the pairs.
p: to all that be in Rome
in every place, theirs and ours

s: the New Testament letters were written as general essays for any reader
they went to real churches and people first: Rome, Corinth, one man named Philemon.
Colossians asks to be read in another church too
cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans.
reading a letter 'as if to you' means forgetting who got it first
context and 'to you' go together: remember Corinth, and let the letter open you too.

games.q: your grandfather reads you a letter his own father wrote him long ago and says, 'this is for you now too.' a cousin says that's silly; it was his letter. how do churches read Paul's letters?
o: only as history, for Corinth and Rome.
as if to whoever opens them, remembering who got them first.
as if Corinth and Rome never mattered.
games.why: 1 Corinthians widens its own address to 'all that in every place', and Colossians asks to be read in the next town. churches read the letters as if to them, without erasing the first readers.

practice: Write a few lines to your future self, on paper if you can. Open the way the letters do: who it's from, who it's to, a word of thanks. Then add one thing you hope that future self still remembers.

wordCard.voice: Block close. The end of the letters read in their own words: mail to real churches, still read as if written to whoever opens it.
